title: Evaluating Generate–Validate–Repair Pipelines for Intent‑to‑Configuration NetOps Tasks: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study comparing a baseline single‑shot LLM configuration generator against a guarded generate→validate→repair pipeline (with a canary stage) on a 1000‑task synthetic NetOps stress corpus (2000 paired episodes). The declared model was gpt-5-mini (provider: openai_responses) and validation used a deterministic digital‑twin validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Under preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics exactly one sampled initial generation per task was deterministically reused by both arms; downstream validation and the permitted single repair call (guarded arm only) were the only mechanisms for paired outcome differences. Results (archived): baseline safe‑deploy = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded safe‑deploy = 1000/1000 = 1.000; paired difference = 0.005 (n11=995, n10=5, n01=0, n00=0). The preregistered primary inferential test (exact two‑sided McNemar) yields p = 0.0625 (not < 0.05). A preregistered secondary descriptive summary (paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI, 10,000 resamples, seed 1729) is [0.001, 0.01]. Only five validator‑triggered repairs occurred and total model calls used = 1005 (shared_initial = 1000; repair = 5). We report the exact McNemar result as the preregistered confirmatory outcome, present the bootstrap CI as a secondary descriptive summary, and interpret the small absolute guarded benefit in light of very sparse discordant counts, high baseline validity, validator scope, and the shared_initial_candidate design.

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation for network operations promises operator productivity gains but risks introducing multi‑device sequence and policy violations: generated command sequences can be syntactically plausible yet semantically unsafe in workflow contexts that require ordered actions, protected fields, and invariants. Prior work documents LLM hallucination and prompt sensitivity for structured outputs and motivates coupling generation with deterministic validators and targeted repairs. We evaluate, under a strict preregistered paired design, whether a guarded generate→validate→repair pipeline with a canary stage improves paired safe‑deploy rates relative to a baseline single‑shot LLM generator when both arms begin from the same sampled initial candidate (shared_initial_candidate semantics). Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered paired experimental design focused on end‑to‑end workflow outcomes and downstream validator effects; (2) an autonomous execution and analysis run with archived manifests and validator traces; (3) an evidence‑grounded interpretation showing a small absolute guarded benefit when baseline validity is already high and repairs are rare, and a discussion of construct and external validity implications.
sections.related_work: Surveys and controlled studies document hallucination, prompt sensitivity, and structured‑output failures in LLMs that affect code and configuration generation [1]. Constrained decoding and schema‑aware methods increase rates of executable outputs in structured domains, though much high‑quality evidence originates outside NetOps [2,3]. Recent NetOps and agentic‑AI system papers describe verifier‑assisted repair, guarded architectures, and the importance of governance, protocol‑mediated execution, and auditability for operational safety; these works report prototype improvement but emphasize dependence on validator fidelity and governance layers [4,5,6]. Our study differs by (a) using a preregistered paired design under shared_initial_candidate semantics so that only downstream validator/repair can create paired differences, and (b) reporting deterministic execution accounting and archived validator traces to ground interpretation.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The study was preregistered as cand-003-stud-001 and frozen prior to any model calls. Design: confirmatory paired binary design with 1000 deterministic tasks drawn from the challenging_workflow_stress_v1 synthetic corpus; each task produced exactly one sampled initial generation that was deterministically reused by both arms (generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate). Explicitly: the experiment did not generate independent first‑pass outputs per condition; baseline reflects the single‑shot initial candidate's native validity, and the guarded arm reports the final outcome after deterministic validation and any allowed single repair attempt. Model and sampling metadata: declared model = gpt-5-mini (provider: openai_responses). The archived execution/model_configuration.json records temperature = null/unset; null/unset is not evidence of deterministic hosted‑model sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. Validator and repair: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (digital‑twin emulator) applied intent‑constraint validation (required command presence/ordering, protected‑field noninterference, workflow policies). Under the preregistered adapter contract the guarded pipeline could invoke at most one validator‑guided repair call per task; repair budget per task = 1. Execution accounting pointers: archived provider‑call accounting and reconciliation are recorded in deterministic_reconciliation.json and execution/model_configuration.json (see archived bundle). Analysis plan: primary inferential test = exact two‑sided McNemar on the 2×2 paired contingency (preregistered H1: guarded > baseline in paired success rate; estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline). Predeclared secondary summaries: paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) and sensitivity analyses treating failed calls as unsafe. Multiplicity: Holm–Bonferroni for secondary hypothesis claims; no post‑hoc deviations occurred.
sections.results: Execution and deterministic accounting: start 2026‑09‑01T06:31:07Z; completion 2026‑09‑01T08:38:57Z. Planned episodes = 2000; completed = 2000; failed episodes = 0; complete pairs = 1000. Provider‑call audit (deterministic_reconciliation.json): hosted_model_call_event_count = 1005, stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 1000, repair = 5, cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false. Observed outcomes (archived analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv): n11 = 995, n10 = 5, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Baseline successes = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded successes = 1000/1000 = 1.000; paired (guarded − baseline) = 0.005. Preregistered primary test (exact two‑sided McNemar): p = 0.0625 (not < 0.05). Preregistered secondary descriptive summary (paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI, 10,000 resamples, seed 1729; analysis_log.jsonl): CI = [0.001, 0.01]. Only five validator‑triggered repairs were executed under the allowed repair budget; total model calls used = 1005 (shared_initial = 1000; repair = 5). Sensitivity (archived contingency, not preregistered as primary): one‑sided exact McNemar p (directional: guarded > baseline) = 0.03125; we present this number labeled explicitly as a preregistered‑adjacent sensitivity result, not a replacement for the preregistered two‑sided test.
sections.discussion: Inferential reconciliation: the preregistered confirmatory result is the exact two‑sided McNemar p = 0.0625 and therefore H1 is not supported at two‑sided α = 0.05. The preregistered bootstrap percentile CI [0.001,0.01] is a secondary descriptive summary. The apparent discordance arises from extremely sparse discordant counts (n10=5, n01=0): exact conditional tests condition on total discordants and compute tail probabilities of observing the observed imbalance, while nonparametric bootstrap percentile intervals approximate the sampling distribution of the paired difference and can exclude zero when a few discordants dominate resamples. Mechanism and operational interpretation: under shared_initial_candidate semantics only downstream validator actions (repair/canary/rollback) could alter paired outcomes; with only five repairs invoked the observed absolute improvement (0.5 percentage points) is mechanistically attributable to a small number of validator interventions. Implications: verifier‑guided safeguards can avert some unsafe outcomes in workflow settings, but measurable marginal gains depend strongly on baseline failure prevalence, validator sensitivity and coverage, permitted repair budget, and task distribution. Validator scope and permissiveness: the deterministic validator enforces required sequences and protected‑field constraints but is an abstraction of operational heterogeneity; archived validator traces (representative examples available in execution/scoring/task-000004-baseline.json and other scoring artifacts) show the validator accepted or rejected candidates based on explicit rule checks. If a validator's rule set is permissive or omits long‑range semantic checks, baseline success may be inflated; this construct validity risk is material and discussed further in Limitations. Design tradeoffs and future work: expand model diversity, increase repair budgets, assess independent first‑pass generation arms, and evaluate across more heterogeneous digital twins and vendor models to map risk–utility tradeoffs for agentic NetOps safeguards.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired study with shared_initial_candidate semantics on a 1000‑task synthetic NetOps stress corpus, a guarded generate→validate→repair pipeline produced a small absolute paired improvement (0.005) over a baseline single‑shot LLM generator; the preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar test did not reach α = 0.05 (p = 0.0625). Only five validator repairs occurred and model calls used = 1005. We report the exact McNemar as the preregistered confirmatory outcome and the bootstrap CI as a secondary descriptive summary (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). These artifact‑grounded results indicate that downstream verifier/repair safeguards can prevent some unsafe outcomes, but measurable marginal gains may be limited when baseline outputs are already highly valid and when the paired design isolates downstream effects. We publish the preregistration, execution manifests, validator traces, and analysis artifacts to support reproducibility and recommend follow‑up studies that broaden models, validator fidelity, repair budgets, and topology heterogeneity to better characterize operational risk–utility tradeoffs.

limitations: Single‑model scope: only the declared model gpt-5-mini was evaluated; results do not generalize across model families or versions.

Synthetic corpus and deterministic validator: tasks come from a synthetic stress corpus and validation used a deterministic digital twin (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); external validity to heterogeneous vendor/legacy environments is limited.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired comparison isolates downstream validator/repair effects only; it does not measure differences that would arise from independent first‑pass generations under alternative prompting or constrained‑generation arms that were not executed.

Low baseline failure prevalence: baseline success = 99.5% limited statistical power to detect large absolute improvements; only five validator repairs were invoked, constraining interpretability of repair efficacy.

Statistical nuance: exact McNemar p = 0.0625 (not <0.05) while the executor's bootstrap percentile CI returned [0.001,0.01]; sparse discordant counts and test choice yield sensitivity to analysis method—interpretation must consider both outcomes. The one‑sided exact McNemar sensitivity p = 0.03125 is reported explicitly as a preregistered‑adjacent sensitivity, not as the preregistered primary result.

Construct validity: the safe‑deploy binary depends on the emulator/validator's specification; semantic/policy correctness across multi‑device emergent properties may be underrepresented in the validator's modeled rule set, which can inflate measured baseline success if coverage is limited.
